Fix a spatial dimension $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, side length $L>0$, and odd integer $N\ge3$. Put $h=L/N$ and $\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$. The periodic grid has index set $J_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$ and nodes $x_j=hj$ modulo $L$. A grid scalar is a real array $u=(u_j)_{j\in J_N}$; a grid vector has $d$ real components at each node. Define
$$ \langle u,v\rangle_h=h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}u_jv_j,\qquad \|u\|_h=\langle u,u\rangle_h^{1/2},\qquad \bar u=L^{-d}h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}u_j . $$ The same pairing is componentwise for grid vectors. For the coordinate vector $e_a$, define the centered field difference and positive periodic Poisson stencil by $$ (D_a^0u)_j=\frac{u_{j+e_a}-u_{j-e_a}}{2h},\qquad (A_hu)_j=\sum_{a=1}^d\frac{2u_j-u_{j+e_a}-u_{j-e_a}}{h^2}. $$
All indices wrap modulo $N$. The discrete Fourier index set is $\mathcal K_N=\{-\frac{N-1}{2},\ldots,\frac{N-1}{2}\}^d$; the character at $k\in\mathcal K_N$ is $j\mapsto e^{2\pi i k\cdot j/N}$. This odd-grid convention has no Nyquist mode.

Two integrations by parts give $\frac h2(f(a)+f(a+h))-\int_a^{a+h}f(x)\,dx=\int_a^{a+h}K(x)f''(x)\,dx .$ Since $K\ge0$ and $\int_a^{a+h}K(x)\,dx=h^3/12$, the absolute cell error is at most $h^3\|f''\|_\infty/12$. Sum over the $N$ periodic cells, whose endpoint contributions assemble into the periodic trapezoid sum $h\sum_j f(jh)$. This gives the one-dimensional error bound $Lh^2\|f''\|_\infty/12$.

For each coordinate $a$, let $Q_a$ denote the periodic trapezoid operator in that coordinate and $I_a$ integration over that coordinate. Both have sup-norm operator bound at most $L$, since their weights are nonnegative and sum to $L$. In the $a$th summand, the one-dimensional bound from step 1.1 applies after the later-coordinate integrations; differentiation in coordinate $a$ commutes with those integrations. The other $d-1$ operators contribute at most $L^{d-1}$ in sup norm. Thus that summand is bounded by $L^dh^2\|\partial_{aa}f\|_\infty/12$. For each position $y\in\mathbb T_L^d$, define the continuous unit-source field by taking the zero-mean solution $\phi_\varepsilon^y$ from [[thm-periodic-pic-continuum-regularized-poisson-kernel-is-smooth]] for $\mu=\delta_y$, and setting
$$ \mathcal E_\varepsilon(x,y)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}\eta_\varepsilon(z-x)(-\nabla\phi_\varepsilon^y(z))\,dz =\frac1{L^d}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}} \frac{-i\kappa_k}{|\kappa_k|^2} \left(\prod_{a=1}^d\alpha_\varepsilon^{2|k_a|}\right)e^{i\kappa_k\cdot(x-y)} . $$ The series converges absolutely with all derivatives by geometric summability. For the grid branch, let $\phi_h^y$ be the mean-zero solution of $$ A_h\phi_h^y=h^{-d}w^{\varepsilon,h}(y)-L^{-d}\mathbf1 $$ whose compatibility follows from [[thm-periodic-pic-charge-conservation-and-neutralized-source]], and put $$ \mathcal E_{\varepsilon,h}(x,y)=\sum_{j\in J_N}w_j^{\varepsilon,h}(x)(-D^0\phi_h^y)_j . $$ If $z=(x,v)$ and $z'=(y,w)$ are lifted phase-space states in $\mathbb R^{2d}$, the continuum and grid mean-field kernels are $$ \mathbb K_\varepsilon(z,z')=(v,cQ\,\mathcal E_\varepsilon(x,y)),\qquad \mathbb K_{\varepsilon,h}(z,z')=(v,cQ\,\mathcal E_{\varepsilon,h}(x,y)). $$
The spatial components are periodic in their position variables. A finite equal-weight system $\dot z_p=P^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^P\mathbb K_{\varepsilon,h}(z_p,z_r)$ uses particle charge $Q/P$ and mass $M/P$. No claim about the limit $\varepsilon\to0$ is part of this definition.

For fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and periodic grid, the smooth-branch weights $w_j^{\varepsilon,h}$ of [[def-periodic-pic-shape-assignment-and-gather]] are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb T_L^d$. For every multi-index $\beta$, $\max_j\|\partial^\beta w_j^{\varepsilon,h}\|_\infty<\infty$. They are nonnegative and sum to one at every point.

For any real grid array $s$, define its mean-zero periodic Poisson pseudoinverse by
$$ A_h^\dagger s:=\text{the unique mean-zero grid array }u\text{ such that }A_hu=s-\bar s\,\mathbf1, $$
where $\bar s=L^{-d}\langle s,\mathbf1\rangle_h$. This definition is well-defined by [[thm-periodic-centered-difference-poisson-zero-mode-and-gauge]]. It gives $A_hA_h^\dagger s=s-\bar s\mathbf1$, $A_h^\dagger\mathbf1=0$, and a linear self-adjoint map on the full finite grid space.

derivations.claim: By [F2], each grid weight is smooth and has bounded derivatives of every finite order. By [F1], $\mathcal E_{\varepsilon,h}$ is a finite sum of products of such weights and fixed matrix entries, so it is $C^\infty$ and all its derivatives are bounded. In particular, both derivative suprema $M_x^{\varepsilon,h},M_y^{\varepsilon,h}$ are finite. More explicitly, if $B_{jk}$ are the vector entries of $-D^0A_h^\dagger$ and $C_w=\max_j\|\nabla w_j\|_\infty$, then $M_x^{\varepsilon,h}\le |cQ|h^{-d}C_w \sum_{j,k}|B_{jk}|\|w_k\|_\infty,\qquad M_y^{\varepsilon,h}\le |cQ|h^{-d}C_w \sum_{j,k}|B_{jk}|\|w_j\|_\infty ,$ which are finite explicit bounds for the defining suprema.

Any finite-order derivative of the continuum series multiplies each coefficient by finitely many components of $\kappa_k$. The coefficient already has one factor $|\kappa_k|^{-1}$; after $r$ additional derivatives, its magnitude is bounded by a constant times $(1+|k|)^r\prod_a\alpha_\varepsilon^{2|k_a|}$. These bounds are summable because each one-dimensional geometric series with a polynomial factor converges. Thus every differentiated series converges uniformly, and all derivatives are bounded. In particular, for a first derivative the factor $|\kappa_k|$ cancels the denominator $|\kappa_k|^2$, so its norm is bounded by the displayed sum times $|cQ|/L^d$. Periodicity permits the same bounds on Euclidean lifts.

First change $z=(x,v)$ while holding $z'=(y,w)$ fixed. The output difference has components $(v-\widetilde v,cQ(\mathcal E_{\varepsilon,h}(x,y)-\mathcal E_{\varepsilon,h}(\widetilde x,y)))$. Its squared Euclidean norm is at most $|v-\widetilde v|^2+(M_x^{\varepsilon,h})^2|x-\widetilde x|^2$, hence its norm is at most $\max\{1,M_x^{\varepsilon,h}\}|z-\widetilde z|$. Next change $z'$ while holding $\widetilde z$ fixed; this changes only the field component, by at most $M_y^{\varepsilon,h}|z'-\widetilde z'|$. Adding these bounds gives the stated two-variable estimate with $L_{\varepsilon,h}$. The same block-norm calculation using the continuum derivative bounds from step 1.2 gives the estimate with $L_\varepsilon$.

$$ \widehat\mu(k)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}e^{-2\pi i k\cdot y/L}\,d\mu(y),\qquad \kappa_k=2\pi k/L . $$ Then $\eta_\varepsilon$ is strictly positive, even, smooth, and has integral one. The regularized neutralized source $$ \rho_\varepsilon^\mu(x)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}\eta_\varepsilon(x-y)\,d\mu(y)-Q/L^d $$ is $C^\infty$ with zero mean. The assignment and centered-stencil Taylor bounds give the residual $r_h=s_h-A_h(\phi_\varepsilon|_h),\qquad \|r_h\|_\infty\le C_{\rm src}h^2 .$ Here [F1] bounds the measure-assignment error by $C_{\rm dep}h^2$, and for each coordinate the centered second difference has remainder at most $h^2\|\partial_a^4\phi_\varepsilon\|_\infty/12$, whose sum is $C_{\rm FD}h^2$.

The weighted grid norm satisfies $\|r_h\|_h\le L^{d/2}\|r_h\|_\infty$ because the grid has $N^d$ points and $h^dN^d=L^d$. In [F3], take $s=s_h$, $\phi=\phi_h$, and $\widetilde\phi=\phi_\varepsilon|_h$; its residual is exactly $r_h$ from step 1.1, so $\|D^0(\phi_h-\phi_\varepsilon|_h)\|_h \le \gamma_{N,L}L^{d/2}C_{\rm src}h^2$. For any nonnegative normalized weights, $\sum_jw_j(x)^2\le1$, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|G_xV|\le h^{-d/2}\|V\|_h$. Apply this to the two grid-field errors in step 2.1. Their gathered contribution is at most $L^{d/2}h^{2-d/2}(\gamma_{N,L}C_{\rm src}+C_3)$.

The remaining difference is gathering the exact nodal samples $E_\varepsilon(x_j)$ instead of the continuous field. Apply the Euclidean-vector bound of [F1] with $m=d$ and $g=E_\varepsilon$. Its translation-uniform constant is exactly $C_{\eta,E}$ in the Statement, so this difference is at most $C_{\rm int}h^2$. The unit-vector projection proof in that supplier introduces no $\sqrt d$ factor. Add this to step 3.1 to get the displayed estimate. Since $\gamma_{N,L}\le L/4$ and $2-d/2>0$ for $d\le3$, both terms tend to zero.

These are finite mesh- and regularization-dependent constants. The phase kernel $\mathbb K_{\varepsilon,h}$ is globally Lipschitz in the two-variable convention $$ |\mathbb K_{\varepsilon,h}(z,z')-\mathbb K_{\varepsilon,h}(\widetilde z,\widetilde z')| \le L_{\varepsilon,h}\bigl(|z-\widetilde z|+|z'-\widetilde z'|\bigr). $$ The continuum kernel $\mathbb K_\varepsilon$ is also globally Lipschitz with the explicit admissible constant $$ L_\varepsilon=\max\left\{1,\frac{|cQ|}{L^d} \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}}\prod_{a=1}^d\alpha_\varepsilon^{2|k_a|}\right\}. $$

Under the smoothness and compact-tube hypotheses of [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]], the forward Euler, explicit midpoint, and classical four-stage tableaus of [[def-euler-midpoint-rk4-tableaus]] have uniform local orders at least one, two, and four, respectively.

For the scalar test equation $y'=\lambda y$, set $z=h\lambda$. The corresponding stability functions, defined by $y^+=R(z)y$, are
$$R_{\mathrm E}(z)=1+z,\qquad R_{\mathrm M}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2},\qquad R_{\mathrm{RK4}}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2}+\frac{z^3}{6}+\frac{z^4}{24}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, and let $M$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. Write $\nabla U$ for its Euclidean gradient, and let $\epsilon>0$.

For $a,b\in\mathbb R$, define the **force kick** and **drift shear**
$$K_a(q,p)=(q,p-a\nabla U(q)),\qquad D_b(q,p)=(q+bM^{-1}p,p).$$
The one-step leapfrog map is
$$\Phi_\epsilon=K_{\epsilon/2}\circ D_\epsilon\circ K_{\epsilon/2},$$
where composition is read right to left. For a finite integer $L\ge1$, its $L$-step map is $\Phi_\epsilon^L$. Define the momentum flip $R(q,p)=(q,-p)$ and the flipped proposal map $T_{\epsilon,L}=R\circ\Phi_\epsilon^L$.

Each kick and drift is a continuous bijection with inverse $K_{-a}$ or $D_{-b}$, respectively. These finite maps use only $\nabla U$ and do not require a solution of Hamilton's ODE. The classical derivative of a force kick is not part of this definition: for merely $U\in C^1$, $\nabla U$ need not be differentiable.

Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $V\in C^2(Q)$, and $M$ be symmetric positive definite. Put $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$. At every point of their open domains, the local kick and drift from [[def-local-leapfrog-domain-on-an-open-configuration-set]] are $C^1$ and their Jacobians $A$ satisfy $A^TJA=J$. Here this matrix identity is the finite-regularity meaning of symplecticity; no smooth-manifold definition is being applied to a map of insufficient regularity.

Under the hypotheses of [[lem-canonical-kick-and-drift-shears-have-symplectic-jacobians]], every admitted local leapfrog step and every admitted kick-then-drift symplectic Euler step is a $C^1$ map with continuous Jacobian satisfying $D\Phi^TJD\Phi=J$ on its open admitted domain. The result concerns symplecticity, not energy conservation.

Let $d\ge1$, $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $V\in C^3(Q)$, and $M$ symmetric positive definite. Set $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$ and $F(q,p)=(M^{-1}p,-\nabla V(q))$. Fix $T>0$ and $h=T/N$ with $N\ge1$. Suppose the exact solution, numerical states, all kick/drift intermediate states, and every line segment used below lie in one compact convex tube $K\Subset Q\times\mathbb R^d$, with the derivatives of $F$ through order two bounded there. For $z_0$ in that tube, write $e_n^E$ for the error of iterated kick-then-drift symplectic Euler and $e_n^V$ for the error of iterated local leapfrog relative to the exact solution at $t_n=nh$. Write $\Psi_h^E$ and $\Psi_h^V$ for their admitted one-step maps and $\varphi_h$ for the exact flow. For sufficiently small $h$, constants $C_E,C_V,L$ independent of $h,N,n$ satisfy
$$\|\Psi_h^E(z)-\varphi_h(z)\|\le C_Eh^2,\qquad \|\Psi_h^V(z)-\varphi_h(z)\|\le C_Vh^3$$
for admitted $z\in K$, and whenever $nh\le T$,
$$e_n^E\le e^{LT}e_0+C_ETe^{LT}h,\qquad e_n^V\le e^{LT}e_0+C_VTe^{LT}h^2.$$
Thus symplectic Euler has global order one and leapfrog has global order two on the stated controlled tube. No unconditional domain-admissibility claim is made.

$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a

derivations.claim: The kicks and drifts in [F1] have inverses $K_{-a}$ and $D_{-b}$. Reversing the composition gives $\Phi_{\Delta t}^{-1}=K_{-\Delta t/2}\circ D_{-\Delta t}\circ K_{-\Delta t/2}=\Phi_{-\Delta t}$. All maps are global on the periodic lift, so no intermediate-domain restriction is lost.

The potential is smooth, hence $C^2$, and $M$ is symmetric positive definite. Each admitted kick and drift satisfies the symplectic Jacobian identity [F2]; composing the three maps preserves that identity by the chain rule, as stated in [F3].

Each is block triangular with identity diagonal blocks, so its determinant is $1$; multiplicativity gives $\det D\Phi_{\Delta t}=1$. The global kick/drift maps are $C^1$ diffeomorphisms, so [A1] permits applying [F5] to the map and its inverse, proving preservation of Lebesgue volume.

Let $N\ge2$ be an integer, let $x_j=2\pi j/N$ for $j=0,\ldots,N-1$, and identify $x_N$ with $x_0$ periodically. The real trigonometric interpolation space is
$$\mathcal T_N= \begin{cases} \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{1,\cos(kx),\sin(kx):1\le k\le (N-1)/2\},&N\text{ odd},\\ \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{1,\cos(kx),\sin(kx):1\le k<N/2\}\oplus\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\cos(Nx/2)\},&N\text{ even}. \end{cases}$$
For real nodal data $U=(U_0,\ldots,U_{N-1})$, define its periodic Fourier interpolant by
$$
I_NU(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}U_jL_j(x),
$$
where, for $N=2K+1$,
$$
L_j(x)=\frac1N\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K}\cos(k(x-x_j))\right),
$$
and, for $N=2K$,
$$
L_j(x)=\frac1N\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\cos(k(x-x_j))+\cos(K(x-x_j))\right).
$$
Thus the even-grid Nyquist component is the real cosine $\cos(Nx/2)$ only. Its sampled derivative is defined by differentiating this interpolant; the resulting Nyquist derivative values are zero at every grid point.

Let $N\ge2$ and $x_j=2\pi j/N$. If integers $k,r$ satisfy $k\equiv r\pmod N$, then
$$
e^{ikx_j}=e^{irx_j}\qquad(0\le j<N).
$$
Consequently, sampling a product of Fourier modes with frequencies $k_1,\ldots,k_s$ gives the same nodal data as the single mode whose frequency is the sum $\sum_{\ell=1}^s k_\ell$ reduced modulo $N$.

The frequency space in [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]] is real-valued. For complex data, let $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ be the space obtained by allowing complex coefficients in that same real basis, and extend its cardinal formula by
$$
I_N^{\mathbb C}V(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}V_jL_j(x),\qquad V\in\mathbb C^N.
$$
Then $I_N^{\mathbb C}V$ is the unique member of $\mathcal T_N^{\mathbb C}$ with nodal data $V$. On real data this formula agrees with $I_N$; in the even case the complex Nyquist samples are interpolated by the real basis function $\cos(Nx/2)$.

Input an integer $N\ge2$ and real data $U_0,\ldots,U_{N-1}$ on the grid of [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]]. Set $K=(N-1)/2$ when $N$ is odd and $K=N/2$ when $N$ is even. Form the $(N\times N)$ matrix
$$(D_N)_{ij}= \begin{cases} -\dfrac2N\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}k\sin(k(x_i-x_j)),&N\text{ odd},\\[1.2ex] -\dfrac2N\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}k\sin(k(x_i-x_j)),&N\text{ even}, \end{cases} \qquad 0\le i,j<N.$$
The algorithm returns $D_N$ and the derivative vector $D_NU$. In the even case it omits the derivative of the Nyquist cosine because $\sin((N/2)(x_i-x_j))=0$ for grid indices $i,j$. All operations are in exact real arithmetic; no floating-point stability or error guarantee is asserted.

Let $N\ge2$, let $U=(U_j)_{j=0}^{N-1}\in\mathbb R^N$, and let $p=I_NU\in\mathcal T_N$ be the interpolant defined in [[def-periodic-fourier-collocation-grid]]. The matrix [[alg-periodic-fourier-collocation-differentiation-matrix]] satisfies
$$
(D_NU)_i=p'(x_i),\qquad 0\le i<N.
$$
For even $N$, this statement includes the Nyquist cosine mode, whose derivative vanishes at the grid nodes.

Fix a spatial dimension $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, side length $L>0$, and odd integer $N\ge3$. Put $h=L/N$ and $\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$. The periodic grid has index set $J_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$ and nodes $x_j=hj$ modulo $L$. A grid scalar is a real array $u=(u_j)_{j\in J_N}$; a grid vector has $d$ real components at each node. Define
$$ \langle u,v\rangle_h=h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}u_jv_j,\qquad \|u\|_h=\langle u,u\rangle_h^{1/2},\qquad \bar u=L^{-d}h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}u_j . $$ The same pairing is componentwise for grid vectors. For the coordinate vector $e_a$, define the centered field difference and positive periodic Poisson stencil by $$ (D_a^0u)_j=\frac{u_{j+e_a}-u_{j-e_a}}{2h},\qquad (A_hu)_j=\sum_{a=1}^d\frac{2u_j-u_{j+e_a}-u_{j-e_a}}{h^2}. $$
All indices wrap modulo $N$. The discrete Fourier index set is $\mathcal K_N=\{-\frac{N-1}{2},\ldots,\frac{N-1}{2}\}^d$; the character at $k\in\mathcal K_N$ is $j\mapsto e^{2\pi i k\cdot j/N}$. This odd-grid convention has no Nyquist mode.

Use the grid, inner product, and operator $A_h$ of [[def-periodic-pic-grid-and-inner-product]]. Then $A_h$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative, $\ker A_h$ consists exactly of constant arrays, and $\operatorname{ran}A_h=\{s:\bar s=0\}$. Consequently, for every compatible source $\bar s=0$, there is a unique solution $\phi$ of $A_h\phi=s$ with the gauge $\bar\phi=0$.

For $k\in\mathcal K_N$, the Fourier character $e_k(j)=e^{2\pi i k\cdot j/N}$ is an eigenvector with
$$ \lambda_h(k)=\frac4{h^2}\sum_{a=1}^d\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k_a}{N}\right). $$
Only $k=0$ has eigenvalue zero.

On the torus and grid of [[def-periodic-pic-grid-and-inner-product]], an algebraic assignment shape is any family of functions $w_j:\mathbb T_L^d\to[0,\infty)$ such that $\sum_{j\in J_N}w_j(x)=1$ for every $x$. For the smooth fixed-$\varepsilon$ branch used in the force-error and ODE results, put $\alpha_\varepsilon=e^{-\varepsilon/L}$ and choose the explicit even periodic kernel
$$ \eta_\varepsilon(x)=L^{-d}\prod_{a=1}^d \frac{1-\alpha_\varepsilon^2}{1-2\alpha_\varepsilon\cos(2\pi x_a/L)+\alpha_\varepsilon^2}. $$ For this smooth branch and each $x\in\mathbb T_L^d$, set $$ Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)=h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}\eta_\varepsilon(x_j-x),\qquad w_j^{\varepsilon,h}(x)=\frac{h^d\eta_\varepsilon(x_j-x)}{Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)}. $$ Each factor in the kernel denominator is positive, so $Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)>0$ and the smooth-branch weights are well-defined. For any algebraic shape family above and finitely many particle positions $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_P)$ with charges $q_1,\ldots,q_P\in\mathbb R$, write $Q=\sum_{p=1}^Pq_p$ and define deposited charge density $$ \rho_j(X)=h^{-d}\sum_{p=1}^Pq_pw_j(X_p)-Q/L^d . $$
For any grid scalar $g$, its potential gather is $(G_Xg)_p=\sum_jw_j(X_p)g_j$. For any grid vector $E$, its field gather is defined componentwise by the same weights, $(G_XE)_p=\sum_jw_j(X_p)E_j$. Let $\eta_\varepsilon$ be the explicit product kernel in [[def-periodic-pic-shape-assignment-and-gather]], with $\alpha_\varepsilon=e^{-\varepsilon/L}\in(0,1)$. Let $\mu$ be a finite signed Borel measure on $\mathbb T_L^d$ with mass $Q$ and total variation $\|\mu\|_{\rm TV}$. Put
$$ \widehat\mu(k)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}e^{-2\pi i k\cdot y/L}\,d\mu(y),\qquad \kappa_k=2\pi k/L . $$ Then $\eta_\varepsilon$ is strictly positive, even, smooth, and has integral one. The regularized neutralized source $$ \rho_\varepsilon^\mu(x)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}\eta_\varepsilon(x-y)\,d\mu(y)-Q/L^d $$ is $C^\infty$ with zero mean. Its unique zero-mean periodic solution of $-\Delta\phi_\varepsilon^\mu=\rho_\varepsilon^\mu$ is the absolutely and uniformly differentiable Fourier series $$ \phi_\varepsilon^\mu(x)=L^{-d}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\left(\prod_{a=1}^d\alpha_\varepsilon^{|k_a|}\right)\widehat\mu(k)} {|\kappa_k|^2}e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x}. $$
For every integer $r\ge0$, all spatial derivative series of order at most $r$ converge absolutely and uniformly; their bounds may depend on $r,\varepsilon,L,\|\mu\|_{\rm TV}$.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and a finite signed Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb T_L^d$ with total mass $Q$. Let $\rho_\varepsilon=\eta_\varepsilon*\mu-Q/L^d$ and let $\phi_\varepsilon$ be its unique zero-mean periodic Poisson potential from [[thm-periodic-pic-continuum-regularized-poisson-kernel-is-smooth]]. Put $E_\varepsilon=-\nabla\phi_\varepsilon$. Use the shape and periodic centered-difference Poisson operator of [[def-periodic-pic-shape-assignment-and-gather]] and [[def-periodic-pic-grid-and-inner-product]]. Let $s_h=P_h^\varepsilon\mu-Q/L^d$, let $A_h\phi_h=s_h$ with $\bar\phi_h=0$, set $E_{h,j}=-D^0\phi_h$, and gather $G_hE_h$ using the same shape. Define
$$ C_{\rm dep}=\frac{C_\eta\|\eta_\varepsilon\|_\infty}{Z_{\min}}\|\mu\|_{\rm TV},\quad C_{\rm FD}=\frac1{12}\sum_{a=1}^d\|\partial_a^4\phi_\varepsilon\|_\infty,\quad C_{\rm src}=C_{\rm dep}+C_{\rm FD}, $$ where $C_\eta,Z_{\min}$ are from [[lem-periodic-pic-shape-partition-and-quadrature-bound]]. Put $$ C_3=\frac16\left(\sum_{a=1}^d\|\partial_a^3\phi_\varepsilon\|_\infty^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad C_{\rm int}=\frac{C_{\eta,E}+\|E_\varepsilon\|_\infty C_\eta}{Z_{\min}}, \quad C_{\eta,E}=\frac{L^d}{12}\sum_{a=1}^d \sup_{x,y\in\mathbb T_L^d}\left|\partial_{y_a y_a}[\eta_\varepsilon(y-x)E_\varepsilon(y)]\right|_2 . $$ For vector fields, $\|V\|_\infty=\sup_x|V(x)|_2$ (the maximum of Euclidean lengths for grid fields); the derivatives in $C_{\eta,E}$ use this same Euclidean norm. Then the source $s_h$ is compatible and $$ \|G_hE_h-\eta_\varepsilon*E_\varepsilon\|_\infty \le L^{d/2}h^{2-d/2}\left(\gamma_{N,L}C_{\rm src}+C_3\right) +C_{\rm int}h^2. $$
The displayed $\gamma_{N,L}$ is the actual finite-grid inverse/derivative norm of [[thm-periodic-pic-poisson-residual-to-gathered-force-bound]] and satisfies $\gamma_{N,L}\le L/4$. Thus for $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ this fixed-$\varepsilon$ force error tends to zero as $h\to0$. Every constant depends on the stated smooth regularized solution and kernel; this is not an $\varepsilon\to0$ estimate.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, and let $M$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. Write $\nabla U$ for its Euclidean gradient, and let $\epsilon>0$.

For $a,b\in\mathbb R$, define the **force kick** and **drift shear**
$$K_a(q,p)=(q,p-a\nabla U(q)),\qquad D_b(q,p)=(q+bM^{-1}p,p).$$
The one-step leapfrog map is
$$\Phi_\epsilon=K_{\epsilon/2}\circ D_\epsilon\circ K_{\epsilon/2},$$
where composition is read right to left. For a finite integer $L\ge1$, its $L$-step map is $\Phi_\epsilon^L$. Define the momentum flip $R(q,p)=(q,-p)$ and the flipped proposal map $T_{\epsilon,L}=R\circ\Phi_\epsilon^L$.

Each kick and drift is a continuous bijection with inverse $K_{-a}$ or $D_{-b}$, respectively. These finite maps use only $\nabla U$ and do not require a solution of Hamilton's ODE. The classical derivative of a force kick is not part of this definition: for merely $U\in C^1$, $\nabla U$ need not be differentiable.
